title: A lookup-heavy key-value front end on six cores run at 90% of capacity
description: The same six-core key-value front end as w14 (lookups, puts with occasional 120 us flushes, replica syncs routed through the put path, 68 us queries due in 300 us, 120 us multigets, batch, scans and 2 us lease renewals) with the same hints, but lookups are now 30% of all requests while costing only 5% of core time, and the service runs at 90% of its capacity instead of about 82%. Traffic still arrives in bursts, but they are short (a quarter of every millisecond at twice the rate of the rest), as in measured datacenter microbursts. At this load nearly every core is busy with a long request most of the time, so the many cheap lookups keep arriving to find long work queued ahead of them, and the order in which a core picks from its queue decides their tail.
changed_from_previous: w14 at 0.9 of capacity instead of about 0.82 (busiest level 104.5k at 51.6 us per request, versus 75k at 65.6), with lookups raised from 13.5% to 30% of requests and the other weights trimmed, and bursts of 1000 us period instead of 4000 (duty 0.25, factor 2 unchanged); work, hints, deadlines, 6 cores and 16 connections unchanged.
notes: Real shapes. Read-dominated key-value caches: in Facebook's memcached pools GETs outnumber SETs by up to 30 to 1 and most requests are small (Atikoglu et al., SIGMETRICS 2012; Nishtala et al., NSDI 2013), so lookups are the most common latency-critical request but a small share of server time; here they are 30% of requests and 4.9% of core time. Writes with occasional log flushes (RocksDB, Cao et al., FAST 2020), replica syncs (Raft-style replication, etcd), batched multigets and lease renewals (Chubby KeepAlives, Burrows, OSDI 2006) are w14's. The weights are invented (only their read-heavy direction follows the traces); real long-tailed service is approximated by constant kinds plus the puts' bimodal flushes. Short bursts follow measured datacenter microbursts, most of which last well under a millisecond (Zhang et al., IMC 2017); the period returns to the ladder's 1000 us (w4-w10) from the 4000 us that w11-w14 scaled up with their 4x work. Capacity, at 99.6 iterations per us (calibration.json): fake work per request get 0.30x680 = 2.048 us + put 0.06x(0.85x400+0.15x12000) = 1.289 + query 0.32x6800 = 21.847 + sync 0.03x12000 = 3.614 + multiget 3.614 + batch 0.07x6800 = 4.779 + scan 4.779 + lease 0.12x170 = 0.205, total 42.18 us (4200.8 iterations); 6 / 42.18 us = 142.3k req/s (129.9k with the calibrated 4 us per request). Levels are sized from w14's measured light-load medians (gen 10 lesson: 83 iterations per us and about 1 us of non-work core time): 4200.8 / 83 + 1 = 51.61 us per request, 6 / 51.61 us = 116.3k req/s. Levels 35k/81k/93k/98k/102k/104.5k are 30.1/69.7/80.0/84.3/87.7/89.9% of 116.3k; busy-phase rate at 104.5k is 167.2k req/s. Why 0.9 is usable under the headline rule: lookups, puts and leases are 47.1% of requests, so fifo's overall median sits near the bottom of the 68 us kinds (about their 6th percentile, w14: 32nd), and the 1000 us bursts build a quarter of w14's backlog per burst. A central-queue simulation (100 us time slice, bursts) whose medians run 5-10% above w13's and w14's measured fifo medians gives fifo overall medians of 89.9 us at 30% and 108 at 90% (this mix with w14's 4000 us bursts: 183 at 90%, and w13 measured 173 at 90%; w14's mix with 1000 us bursts: 126), against a limit of 1.5 x 91 = 136.5. Hints are w14's, unchanged, so p13's unit stays 4: 49% of HIGH requests carry 400 us or more. Deadlines as in w14: leases 100 us, queries 300 (4.4x), gets, puts and syncs 400, multigets 1200; all at least 3x the kind's work. FIFO penalty: gets wait behind queries, syncs, flushes and multigets. No run.py changes are needed. Prediction at 104.5k: fifo overall median about 100-120 us, fifo get p99 about 450-600 us; sjf_upper get p99 about 200-260 us with get runqueue-wait p99 about 120-170 us (share 0.55-0.68); the same simulation gives the champion fewer urgent-query passes than on w14 (0.4 against 1.1 per ms), so more of the gets' wait comes from every core being busy with long work.
